ENT / AUDIOVESTIBULAR__Otology & Audiove:
Otoscopy is the direct visual examination of the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane (TM) using a handheld otoscope. It is a core bedside ENT skill used to diagnose middle-ear and canal pathology, and to inspect the drum for perforation, effusion, retraction or a mass.

1Indication & principle

Otoscopy is indicated for any ear symptom and forms part of the routine ENT examination.

Otalgia — distinguish otitis externa from otitis media, and exclude a foreign body.
Otorrhoea (discharge) — identify perforation, chronic suppurative otitis media or a canal infection.
Hearing loss — look for wax, effusion, perforation or a retraction pocket.
Routine / screening — a translucent drum with normal landmarks reassures.

The principle is simple magnified illumination: the drum is semi-transparent, so colour, contour and mobility reveal the state of the air-filled middle ear behind it.

2How it is performed — technique
Choose the largest speculum that fits comfortably for the best light and view.
Straighten the canal: pull the pinna up and back in adults, and down and back in children (the infant canal is short and angled).
Hold the otoscope like a pen and brace the little finger against the cheek, so a sudden head movement moves the scope with the patient and avoids canal trauma.
Examine the asymptomatic ear first, inspect the canal as you advance, then focus on the drum.
3Interpretation — the normal drum & abnormal patterns

The normal TM is pearly-grey and translucent with a cone of light antero-inferiorly, the handle of malleus running down to the central umbo, a taut inferior pars tensa and a small superior pars flaccida (attic).

Bulging red/yellow TM + fever, loss of light reflex→Acute otitis media
Retracted, dull TM with fluid level or air bubbles→Otitis media with effusion (glue ear)
Attic / pars flaccida retraction pocket with keratin or crust→Cholesteatoma — refer
Perforation with chronic / pulsatile mucopurulent discharge→Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM)
Oedematous canal full of debris + pain on tragal pressure→Otitis externa
🔦Cone of light
Antero-inferior reflection; lost when drum bulges or retracts.
🦴Handle of malleus
Runs supero-anteriorly from the central umbo toward the lateral process; key orientation landmark.
🥁Pars tensa
Large taut inferior part; site of most perforations.
⚠️Pars flaccida
Small attic region; retraction pockets here harbour cholesteatoma.
4Pneumatic otoscopy, pitfalls & safety

Pneumatic otoscopy uses a rubber bulb to insufflate air and assess TM mobility: a healthy drum moves briskly, while an immobile drum suggests an effusion or perforation. It is the most useful bedside adjunct for diagnosing glue ear.

Wax obstruction is the commonest reason for a failed view — do not report a normal drum you never saw.
A bright light and correct focus are essential; too small a speculum gives a poor view and canal pain.
Discharge may need gentle micro-suction (aural toilet) before the drum is visible.
🚩 Never dismiss an attic crust or retraction pocket as "just wax" — it may conceal a cholesteatoma, which erodes bone and can cause intracranial complications; refer to ENT. Do NOT syringe or irrigate an ear when the TM may be perforated, as this can drive infection into the middle ear and worsen hearing loss.
🎓 The cone of light points antero-inferiorly — use it to orient every drum. Remember the pinna pull: up-and-back in adults, down-and-back in children.

The tuning-fork tests (Rinne and Weber) are quick bedside screens that use a 512 Hz fork to compare air conduction (AC) with bone conduction (BC) and to detect lateralisation of sound. Together they distinguish conductive from sensorineural hearing loss and guide whether formal audiometry or imaging is needed.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used at the bedside to characterise any hearing loss or asymmetry noted on history or whisper test. The physiological basis is a comparison of two pathways to the cochlea:

Air conduction (AC): sound travels ear canal → tympanic membrane → ossicles → cochlea. Depends on an intact conductive apparatus.
Bone conduction (BC): vibration passes through the skull directly to the cochlea, bypassing the middle ear.

Normally AC > BC because the middle ear amplifies sound. A 512 Hz fork is standard: low enough to sustain a long tone, high enough not to be felt as vibration (128/256 Hz give false results by being sensed as touch).

2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
🧪Rinne test
Struck fork placed on the mastoid process (BC); when no longer heard, move prongs beside the external meatus (AC). Ask which was louder. Repeat each ear.
🧪Weber test
Struck fork placed on the midline vertex or forehead (or central incisors). Ask where the sound is heard: centrally, or lateralised to one ear.
Rinne positive (normal): AC > BC — the fork is heard louder/longer at the meatus than on the mastoid.
Rinne negative (abnormal): BC > AC — the fork is heard louder on the mastoid.
3INTERPRETATION
Rinne POSITIVE both ears + Weber CENTRAL→Normal hearing (or symmetric sensorineural loss)
Rinne NEGATIVE one ear (BC>AC) + Weber lateralises TO that ear→Conductive hearing loss on that side (e.g. wax, effusion, otosclerosis)
Rinne POSITIVE + Weber lateralises AWAY from the affected ear→Sensorineural hearing loss on the affected (quieter) side
Rinne NEGATIVE in a profoundly deaf (“dead”) ear→FALSE-negative — sound crosses the skull and is heard by the opposite cochlea

Weber lateralises towards a conductive loss (that ear is shielded from masking background noise and hears bone-conducted sound better) and away from a sensorineural loss (the healthy cochlea wins).

4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
False-negative Rinne: in a dead ear BC is “heard” only because the vibration reaches the contralateral working cochlea — mimics conductive loss. Always cross-check with Weber and audiometry.
Screening only: tuning-fork tests detect a conductive gap of roughly ≥ 15–25 dB; small losses are missed. They do not quantify loss — pure-tone audiometry does.
Wrong fork: 128/256 Hz forks are felt as vibration and give unreliable results; always use 512 Hz.
🚩 A unilateral sensorineural pattern (Weber lateralising AWAY from the poorer-hearing ear, or an asymmetric audiogram) mandates MRI of the internal auditory meatus to exclude an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma). Sudden-onset SNHL over ≤ 72 hours is an ENT emergency requiring urgent audiogram and steroids.
🎓 Remember the direction: Weber lateralises TO the Conductive loss and AWAY from the Sensorineural loss. Always use the 512 Hz fork, and combine Rinne + Weber — neither is interpretable alone.

Pure-tone audiometry (PTA) is the gold-standard subjective test of hearing. It plots the quietest sound a patient can reliably detect (their threshold, in decibels hearing level, dB HL) across the speech-and-beyond frequency range of 250 Hz to 8 kHz, separately for air conduction and bone conduction in each ear. By comparing the two pathways it not only quantifies the degree of hearing loss but classifies it as conductive, sensorineural or mixed, guiding the entire ENT and audiology work-up.

1Indication & principle

Used to objectively quantify and characterise any suspected hearing loss, monitor progression, screen for occupational (noise) damage, and assess candidacy for hearing aids or surgery. The principle rests on two independent pathways to the cochlea:

Air conduction (AC) tests the whole pathway: outer ear → middle ear → cochlea → nerve.
Bone conduction (BC) bypasses the outer and middle ear, vibrating the skull to stimulate the cochlea directly, so it isolates cochlear/neural (sensorineural) function.
The difference between them — the air–bone gap — localises the lesion.

0 dB HL is the average threshold of a healthy young adult, not silence; the scale is referenced to normal hearing, not sound pressure.

2How it is performed

Conducted in a soundproof booth to remove background noise. The patient responds (button/hand) each time a tone is heard, and the audiologist finds the threshold at each frequency using a 10-down, 5-up bracketing method.

Air conduction is delivered by headphones or insert earphones.
Bone conduction is delivered by an oscillator placed on the mastoid process.
Masking: a narrow-band noise is played into the non-test ear to stop it “hearing” a loud tone meant for the poorer ear (cross-hearing), which would otherwise give a falsely good result.

Results are plotted on an audiogram: frequency (Hz) on the x-axis, threshold (dB HL) on the y-axis with quiet at the top — so lower on the chart means worse hearing.

3Interpretation

First decide if there is loss, then read the air–bone relationship, then the shape of the curve:

Thresholds ≤ 20 dB HL→Normal hearing
Thresholds > 20 dB HL→Hearing loss present
BC normal, AC worse — air–bone GAP >10 dB→Conductive loss (outer/middle ear, e.g. wax, effusion, otosclerosis)
AC and BC both elevated together, NO gap→Sensorineural loss (cochlea/nerve)
Bilateral notch at 4 kHz (recovery at 8 kHz)→Noise-induced hearing loss
Down-sloping high-frequency SNHL in an elderly patient→Presbycusis
Fluctuating LOW-frequency SNHL→Ménière’s disease

Severity is graded on the average AC threshold across 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 kHz:

🟢Mild
21–40 dB HL
🟡Moderate
41–70 dB HL
🟠Severe
71–90 dB HL
🔴Profound
> 90 dB HL
4Pitfalls & limitations
Subjective test: depends on patient attention and honesty — unreliable in young children, malingerers or those with cognitive impairment, where objective tests (OAEs, ABR) are needed.
Masking errors are the commonest technical pitfall: under-masking gives a shadow curve from the better ear; over-masking depresses the true threshold.
Collapsing ear canals under headphones can mimic a false conductive gap — insert earphones avoid this.
PTA tests only up to 8 kHz and gives thresholds, not speech discrimination, which needs separate speech audiometry.
🚩 An asymmetric sensorineural loss (>15 dB difference between ears at two adjacent frequencies), or unilateral tinnitus/SNHL, must be investigated with an MRI of the internal auditory meatus (IAM) to exclude a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma).
🎓 Two audiogram sound-bites win marks: an air–bone gap = conductive loss, and a bilateral 4 kHz notch = noise-induced loss.

Tympanometry is an objective, quantitative test of middle-ear function that measures the compliance (admittance) of the tympanic membrane and ossicular chain as the pressure in the sealed ear canal is varied. It requires no active patient response, making it invaluable in children and non-cooperative patients, and is the bedside/clinic gold standard for detecting middle-ear effusion, Eustachian tube dysfunction and tympanic membrane perforation. It is usually performed alongside the stapedial (acoustic) reflex, which probes the integrity of the reflex arc from the cochlea through the auditory nerve, brainstem and facial (VII) nerve to the stapedius muscle.

1Indication & principle

The middle ear transmits sound most efficiently when the pressure on both sides of the tympanic membrane (TM) is equal. Compliance is maximal at this point, so measuring the pressure at which the TM is most mobile reveals the state of the middle-ear cavity.

Used to investigate suspected middle-ear effusion (glue ear / otitis media with effusion), a retracted or perforated TM, Eustachian tube dysfunction, and to check patency of a grommet.
A probe delivers a continuous 226 Hz tone while a pump sweeps ear-canal pressure, typically from +200 to −400 daPa; a microphone records how much sound is reflected versus admitted.
Maximum admittance occurs when canal pressure matches middle-ear pressure — the position of this peak is the diagnostic clue.
2How it is performed
Otoscopy first to exclude wax occlusion or foreign body, which invalidate the seal.
A snug probe tip creates an airtight seal in the external canal; the patient sits still and avoids swallowing or talking during the sweep.
The machine plots a tympanogram (compliance on the y-axis against pressure on the x-axis) and reports the ear-canal volume (ECV), peak pressure and peak compliance.
For the stapedial reflex, a loud tone (~70–100 dB above threshold) is presented and the resulting reflex contraction of stapedius stiffens the ossicular chain, producing a measurable transient drop in admittance.
3Interpretation — Jerger types
Type A — peak at 0 daPa, normal compliance→Normal middle ear
Type B — flat trace, no peak, NORMAL canal volume→Middle-ear effusion (glue ear)
Type B — flat trace, LARGE canal volume→TM perforation or patent grommet
Type C — peak at negative pressure (< −100 daPa)→Eustachian tube dysfunction / TM retraction
Stapedial reflex present & symmetrical→Intact cochlea–VIII–brainstem–VII–stapedius arc
Reflex decay (rapid amplitude fall within 10 s)→Suggests retrocochlear lesion (e.g. vestibular schwannoma)
🧪Ossicular fixation
Absent reflex (e.g. otosclerosis stiffening the stapes)
🧪VII nerve palsy
Absent reflex on the affected side (efferent limb fails)
🧪Severe SNHL
Reflex absent as the stimulus cannot reach threshold
🧪Retrocochlear lesion
Reflex decay — prompt for MRI internal acoustic meatus
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Wax, a poor seal, crying or a very narrow canal produce artefactual flat or noisy traces — always correlate with otoscopy.
A single low reading does not diagnose glue ear; NICE advises repeating tympanometry after an interval (watchful waiting ~3 months) before considering grommets in children.
Tympanometry measures middle-ear mechanics, not hearing thresholds — it complements but does not replace pure-tone audiometry.
🚩 A flat Type B trace with a LARGE ear-canal volume indicates a TM perforation or patent grommet, NOT an effusion — do not misread it and do not attempt to instil ototoxic drops or syringe such an ear. Likewise, absent stapedial reflexes or reflex decay may be the first sign of retrocochlear pathology (e.g. acoustic neuroma) and warrant MRI rather than reassurance.
🎓 Remember the pattern: Type B flat + normal volume = effusion; Type B flat + large volume = perforation/grommet; Type C negative peak = Eustachian tube dysfunction. Ear-canal volume is the discriminator that separates a perforation from a simple effusion.

Positional testing is the bedside method for diagnosing benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) — brief attacks of spinning vertigo lasting seconds, triggered by head movement such as rolling over in bed, lying down or looking up. The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre provokes and identifies posterior canal BPPV (by far the commonest), while the supine roll (Pagnini-McClure) test is used when Dix-Hallpike is negative but horizontal-canal BPPV is suspected. Both work by moving the offending semicircular canal into a gravity-dependent plane so displaced otoconia trigger a characteristic, time-limited nystagmus.

1Indication & principle

Use positional testing for episodic rotatory vertigo lasting seconds that is reliably provoked by a change in head position — turning over in bed, tipping the head back, or bending down. In BPPV, dislodged otoconia (canaliths) from the utricle fall into a semicircular canal; a provoking head movement makes them move under gravity, deflecting the cupula and generating a brief burst of vertigo and nystagmus.

Attacks are positional and transient (typically <60 s), never constant.
Hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness are absent — their presence points elsewhere.
Posterior canal is involved in ~85–90% of cases; horizontal canal accounts for most of the rest.
2Dix-Hallpike technique

Warn the patient it may briefly reproduce their vertigo, and keep their eyes open throughout so you can watch for nystagmus.

Seat the patient upright on the couch, positioned so that when supine the head will extend beyond the top edge.
Turn the head 45° toward the test ear.
Rapidly lay them supine, keeping the 45° rotation, so the head hangs ~20° below horizontal over the edge.
Hold the position and observe the eyes for 30–45 s, then slowly return to sitting and repeat on the other side.

The supine roll (Pagnini-McClure) test is performed if Dix-Hallpike is negative: lie the patient flat with head flexed ~30°, then rapidly turn the whole head 90° to one side and observe, return to centre, and repeat to the other side.

3Interpretation
Latency of a few seconds, then transient up-beating TORSIONAL nystagmus that fatigues on repeat→Posterior canal BPPV on the tested (lowermost) side
Positive Dix-Hallpike→Treat immediately with the Epley (canalith repositioning) manoeuvre
Horizontal, direction-changing nystagmus on the supine roll test→Horizontal (lateral) canal BPPV — worse side localises to the stronger nystagmus
No latency, persistent, non-fatiguing, purely vertical or direction-changing nystagmus→Central cause — arrange neuro-imaging
🧪Latency
BPPV nystagmus starts after a few seconds; central starts at once
⏱️Duration
BPPV is transient (<60 s); central is persistent
🔁Fatigability
BPPV weakens on repeat testing; central does not fatigue
🌀Direction
Posterior-canal BPPV is up-beating torsional; pure vertical suggests central
4Pitfalls & limitations
A single negative test does not exclude BPPV — symptoms are intermittent, so repeat if suspicion is high.
Fixation can suppress nystagmus; Frenzel goggles (removing visual fixation) increase sensitivity.
Neck extension may be limited by cervical spondylosis; a side-lying (Semont) variant can be used.
Vertebrobasilar symptoms or significant carotid/vertebral disease are relative contraindications.
🚩 Nystagmus that is persistent, non-fatiguing, purely vertical/down-beating, or direction-changing — or any accompanying neurological signs (limb ataxia, dysarthria, diplopia, new headache) — indicates a central lesion (e.g. cerebellar stroke). Arrange urgent neuro-imaging and do not attribute to BPPV. Avoid Dix-Hallpike in significant carotid/vertebral disease, cervical instability or an unstable neck.
🎓 Remember the peripheral signature: Latency, Transient, Fatigable, Torsional up-beat = BPPV. The opposite — no latency, persistent, non-fatiguing, purely vertical — is central until proven otherwise.

MRI of the internal auditory meatus (IAM) is a targeted, high-resolution scan of the internal auditory canals and cerebellopontine angles (CPA), performed with gadolinium contrast, to look for a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma). It is the definitive investigation whenever a patient presents with a unilateral (asymmetric) audiovestibular picture — the classic red-flag combination of one-sided sensorineural hearing loss, unilateral tinnitus, or unilateral vestibular failure — because even a tiny nerve tumour can produce these symptoms while remaining invisible on other tests.

1Indication & principle

A vestibular schwannoma arises from the Schwann cells of the vestibular division of the eighth cranial nerve, typically within the bony internal auditory canal. Because it compresses the cochlear and vestibular fibres asymmetrically, the hallmark is a one-sided deficit rather than the symmetrical loss of age-related or noise-induced disease.

Asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) — the single most common presenting feature.
Unilateral tinnitus.
Unilateral vestibular failure — imbalance/disequilibrium rather than acute vertigo.
Late/large tumour: reduced corneal reflex and facial numbness (trigeminal, CN V), then facial weakness (CN VII).

MRI IAM is the gold standard because gadolinium-enhanced T1 imaging demonstrates even small intracanalicular schwannomas that CT misses, and it images the whole CPA cistern.

2How it is performed

Thin-slice sequences are focused on the IAM and CPA. High-resolution heavily T2-weighted images (e.g. CISS/FIESTA) show the nerves as dark filling defects within bright cerebrospinal fluid, while post-gadolinium T1 sequences make an enhancing tumour light up brightly.

Screening can be done without contrast using high-resolution T2, but gadolinium T1 is the reference standard and characterises the lesion.
Check the patient has no MRI contraindication (e.g. certain pacemakers, cochlear implants, metallic foreign bodies) and adequate renal function before gadolinium.
Both canals are imaged for direct side-to-side comparison and to detect bilateral disease.
3Interpretation
Enhancing lesion in the IAM/CPA widening the canal→Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)
"Ice-cream-cone" appearance (intracanalicular stalk + rounded CPA component)→Classic acoustic neuroma morphology
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas→Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) — diagnostic
Enhancing CPA lesion with facial nerve involvement→Consider facial schwannoma or other CPA tumour (e.g. meningioma)
Loss of corneal reflex / facial numbness→Large tumour compressing the trigeminal nerve
🧠Vestibular schwannoma
CN VIII tumour; enhances with gadolinium; ice-cream-cone sign
🧬NF2
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are pathognomonic
🌙Meningioma
CPA differential; broad dural base, dural tail, off-centre from IAM
😐Facial schwannoma
Enhancing lesion tracking along CN VII; early facial weakness
4Pitfalls & limitations
Symptoms correlate poorly with tumour size — a small intracanalicular tumour can cause marked hearing loss, so normal-looking canals on CT never exclude it.
Gadolinium avoided or used cautiously in severe renal impairment; high-resolution T2 screening is an alternative.
Post-operative or post-radiotherapy enhancement can mimic residual tumour on follow-up.
A meningioma or epidermoid may masquerade as a schwannoma; morphology (dural tail, absence of IAM widening) helps distinguish them.
🚩 Any asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss or unilateral tinnitus must be investigated with MRI IAM to exclude a vestibular schwannoma. A missed tumour can grow to compress the brainstem and cerebellum, and bilateral tumours signal neurofibromatosis type 2 requiring genetic and family assessment.
🎓 Unilateral SNHL or unilateral tinnitus → think MRI IAM. The classic radiological sign is the "ice-cream-cone" (intracanalicular stalk with a rounded CPA scoop), and bilateral vestibular schwannomas are diagnostic of NF2.
The acute-vertigo and objective-hearing tests that complete the audiovestibular work-up.
1Acute vestibular syndrome: HINTS
  • For continuous vertigo (not positional): Head impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew.
  • Peripheral (e.g. vestibular neuronitis): positive head impulse (corrective saccade) + unidirectional horizontal nystagmus + no skew.
  • Central (stroke until proven otherwise): normal head impulse, OR direction-changing/vertical nystagmus, OR skew deviation → urgent stroke imaging (HINTS beats early MRI). Vertigo › Stroke/TIA ›
2Objective hearing tests
  • OAEs test outer hair cells; UK newborn screening = automated OAE → automated ABR (two-stage) → audiology referral.
  • ABR gives objective thresholds when PTA is unreliable (neonates, non-cooperative) and screens for retrocochlear disease. Hearing loss ›
Caloric testing→irrigate the ear warm/cold — COWS (Cold-Opposite, Warm-Same, for fast-phase nystagmus); reduced/absent = canal paresis (peripheral vestibular hypofunction); also used in coma/brainstem-death testing.
Conductive air-bone gap + bone-conduction dip at 2 kHz→Carhart notch = otosclerosis → ENT for stapedectomy or hearing aid.
Sudden SNHL over ≤72 h→ENT emergency — confirm on PTA (≥30 dB over 3 contiguous frequencies), high-dose oral ± intratympanic steroids, and MRI IAM to exclude a schwannoma.
🎓 Exam pearl. HINTS: normal head impulse / vertical or direction-changing nystagmus / skew = central (stroke). Newborn screen = OAE → ABR. Carhart notch = otosclerosis. Sudden SNHL = emergency (steroids).
ENT / AUDIOVESTIBULAR__Head & Neck / Rhi:
High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the temporal bone is the first-line cross-sectional investigation for chronic ear disease. Using sub-millimetre bone-window slices, it maps the intricate osseous anatomy of the middle ear and skull base to answer two clinical questions: is there a cholesteatoma eroding the ossicles and attic, and in the unwell diabetic or immunocompromised patient, is there necrotising (malignant) otitis externa with skull-base osteomyelitis?

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE
Chronic malodorous ear discharge, a retraction pocket or attic crust, or conductive hearing loss suggesting cholesteatoma — CT defines disease extent and bony erosion before surgery.
Elderly/diabetic or immunocompromised patient with severe, unremitting otalgia, otorrhoea and granulation tissue on the canal floor — raises necrotising otitis externa.
HRCT is chosen because its exquisite bony detail resolves the ossicles, scutum, tegmen tympani, facial (fallopian) canal and skull base — the very structures these diseases destroy.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Non-contrast HRCT with thin (0.5–1 mm) slices reconstructed on a bone algorithm in axial and coronal planes; the coronal view best shows the scutum, Prussak space and tegmen.
No specific patient preparation is required; it is quick and does not need contrast to demonstrate bony erosion.
MRI (with diffusion-weighted imaging) is added when soft-tissue characterisation is needed — DWI shows restricted diffusion in cholesteatoma and helps detect intracranial complications; nuclear imaging (technetium/gallium) supports diagnosis and follow-up of skull-base osteomyelitis.
3INTERPRETATION
Soft-tissue mass in the attic (Prussak space) with scutum blunting & ossicular erosion→Cholesteatoma
Erosion / dehiscence of the tegmen tympani→Risk of intracranial extension (meningitis, abscess)
Erosion of the lateral (horizontal) semicircular canal→Labyrinthine fistula — cholesteatoma complication (vertigo, positive fistula test)
Skull-base osteomyelitis / bony erosion in an elderly diabetic with Pseudomonas→Necrotising (malignant) otitis externa
🦴Scutum
Sharp bony spur; blunting is an early sign of attic cholesteatoma
⚙️Ossicles
Malleus/incus erosion causes conductive hearing loss
🧠Tegmen tympani
Roof of middle ear; erosion opens a route to the cranial cavity
😐Facial canal
Dehiscence predicts risk of facial nerve palsy
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
CT cannot reliably distinguish cholesteatoma from non-specific granulation tissue, fluid or scar — all appear as soft-tissue opacity; DWI-MRI resolves this ambiguity.
In early necrotising otitis externa CT may be normal because 30–50% of bone mineral must be lost before erosion is visible; a normal CT does not exclude it — correlate with nuclear imaging and inflammatory markers.
Post-operative or post-radiotherapy changes can mimic disease, so imaging must be read alongside the clinical picture and otoscopy.
🚩 Necrotising (malignant) otitis externa is a life-threatening skull-base osteomyelitis, usually Pseudomonas aeruginosa in diabetics/immunocompromised patients. It demands urgent CT/nuclear imaging, prolonged IV anti-pseudomonal antibiotics (e.g. ciprofloxacin/piperacillin–tazobactam), tight glycaemic control and ENT admission. Untreated cholesteatoma likewise erodes bone and can cause facial palsy, labyrinthine fistula, meningitis and intracranial abscess — never dismiss chronic foul discharge.
🎓 Two pattern-recognition anchors: Cholesteatoma = attic (Prussak-space) soft tissue with scutum blunting and ossicular erosion on CT. Necrotising OE = elderly diabetic, granulation tissue on the canal floor, Pseudomonas, skull-base erosion.

Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology (USS-FNAC) is the pivotal first-line investigation for a persistent neck lump. Real-time ultrasound characterises the node (size, shape, hilum, vascularity, cystic/necrotic change) and steers the needle into the most abnormal region to obtain a representative sample, allowing rapid triage of a lump as reactive, metastatic squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), thyroid malignancy or possible lymphoma while preserving the surgical field for any later neck dissection.

1Indication & principle

An unexplained neck lump (especially in those aged 45 and over) persisting beyond ~3–6 weeks warrants urgent assessment on the 2-week-wait head-and-neck pathway. USS-FNAC is the recommended first investigation for suspected metastatic head-and-neck SCC, a suspicious thyroid nodule, or to characterise nodal disease.

Ultrasound is operator-friendly, radiation-free and characterises benign (fatty hilum, oval shape) versus suspicious (round, necrotic) nodes.
Aspiration cytology samples cells for the pathologist; guidance ensures the needle samples solid/abnormal tissue rather than a cystic centre or normal fat.
2How it is performed

The patient lies supine with the neck extended. Under sterile prep and real-time ultrasound, a fine (23–25G) needle is passed into the target lesion; several to-and-fro passes with gentle suction or capillary action aspirate cellular material. Smears are made onto slides (air-dried and alcohol-fixed) and sent for cytology; rapid on-site evaluation (ROSE) can confirm adequacy. Local anaesthetic is usually unnecessary and pressure is applied afterwards.

Cystic nodes are aspirated from the solid mural component for diagnostic yield.
Ultrasound documents node level, size and internal architecture to guide staging.
3Interpretation
Round node, loss of fatty hilum, cystic/necrotic change, peripheral (capsular) vascularity→Sonographically suspicious for malignancy
Cystic level II node in an adult→Think HPV-related oropharyngeal (tonsil/base of tongue) SCC metastasis
FNAC shows squamous cells→Metastatic SCC — seek the primary (examination + panendoscopy ± cross-sectional imaging)
FNAC shows a lymphoid population but is equivocal→Proceed to CORE or excisional biopsy — FNAC cannot subtype lymphoma
🧪Squamous cells
Metastatic SCC — hunt the mucosal primary
🦋Thyroid follicular cells
Reported by Thy category (Thy1–5)
🧬Lymphoid population
Cannot subtype — needs core/excision
🦠Necrotic/granulomatous
Consider TB — send for culture
4Pitfalls & limitations
A non-diagnostic (inadequate) sample does not exclude malignancy — repeat FNA or escalate to core biopsy.
Sampling error: aspirating the cystic centre of a necrotic metastasis can yield only debris and a false-negative.
FNAC gives cytology only, without architecture — it cannot distinguish reactive hyperplasia from low-grade lymphoma.
🚩 FNAC cannot reliably diagnose or subtype LYMPHOMA — if lymphoma is suspected, obtain a core or excisional biopsy for architecture and immunophenotyping. Conversely, never excise a neck node as the first step when metastatic SCC is possible: excision breaches tissue planes, seeds tumour and compromises later neck dissection. Always image and FNA first.
🎓 A neck lump in an adult is malignant until proven otherwise. USS-FNAC is the first-line diagnostic step; squamous cells mean metastatic SCC and trigger a search for the primary, whereas suspected lymphoma needs core or excisional biopsy rather than FNAC.

Salivary gland imaging investigates recurrent gland swelling, suspected obstruction (stones or strictures), inflammatory conditions and masses of the parotid and submandibular glands. Ultrasound (USS) is the first-line modality — it detects calculi, ductal dilatation and gland lesions, and guides fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC). Sialography, which injects contrast into the salivary duct to outline ductal anatomy, is reserved for delineating strictures and radiolucent calculi and is avoided during acute infection.

1Indication & principle

The classic trigger for imaging is recurrent, meal-related gland swelling: eating stimulates salivary flow, and an obstructed duct causes painful distension that settles between meals. This pattern strongly suggests an obstructing calculus or stricture.

Recurrent submandibular/parotid swelling, especially at mealtimes → obstruction (stone or stricture).
Acute painful swelling with pus at the duct orifice → sialadenitis (often superimposed on a stone).
Diffuse bilateral gland enlargement → think Sjögren syndrome or chronic sialadenitis.
A discrete lump in the gland → neoplasm requiring characterisation and FNAC.
2How it is performed

Ultrasound: a high-frequency linear probe is placed over the gland; no preparation is needed. It assesses gland echotexture, ductal calibre, calculi (hyperechoic with posterior acoustic shadowing) and any focal mass, and can guide needle sampling in real time.

Sialography: the duct orifice (Wharton duct in the floor of the mouth for the submandibular gland; Stensen duct opposite the upper 2nd molar for the parotid) is cannulated and iodinated contrast injected under fluoroscopy to outline the ductal tree. It demonstrates strictures, ductal architecture and filling defects from radiolucent stones.

🧪Ultrasound
First-line; stones, ductal dilatation, masses, guides FNAC
💉Sialography
Contrast ductogram; strictures, ductal anatomy, radiolucent calculi
🔬FNAC
USS-guided sampling to characterise a solid mass
3Interpretation

Match the imaging finding to the clinical picture:

Meal-related submandibular swelling + hyperechoic focus with acoustic shadow on USS→Submandibular (Wharton duct) calculus
Dilated duct proximal to a filling defect on sialography→Obstructing stone or ductal stricture
Diffuse gland enlargement with sialectasis (punctate contrast pooling)→Sjögren syndrome or chronic sialadenitis
Solid, well-defined parotid mass→USS + FNAC (pleomorphic adenoma vs Warthin vs malignancy)
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Small or non-calcified stones may be missed on USS; deep parotid or floor-of-mouth stones can be hard to visualise.
Sialography is operator-dependent, requires a patent orifice and uses iodinated contrast — caution with contrast allergy.
USS is limited for the deep lobe of the parotid and cannot fully stage malignancy — MRI is used to assess deep extension and perineural spread.
A radiolucent stone invisible on plain film may still be shown as a filling defect on sialography or a shadowing focus on USS.
🚩 Do NOT perform sialography during acute sialadenitis — retrograde contrast injection can worsen infection or perforate an inflamed duct. A parotid mass with facial nerve weakness, pain, fixation or rapid growth suggests malignancy and warrants urgent 2-week-wait referral.
🎓 Around 80% of salivary calculi arise in the submandibular gland/Wharton duct (its saliva is more viscous and mucin-rich, and drainage is uphill). Meal-time swelling = obstruction; USS is first-line, and sialography is avoided in acute sialadenitis.

Anterior rhinoscopy is a bedside examination of the nasal cavity using a nasal speculum and a good light source. In the context of epistaxis (nosebleed) it lets you identify the source of bleeding, distinguish an anterior from a posterior bleed, inspect the septum and turbinates, and detect sinister causes such as a sinonasal mass. It is the single most important first step in triaging the bleeding nose because it directs whether simple cautery will suffice or whether admission and packing are required.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used to assess acute or recurrent epistaxis, nasal obstruction, and to inspect the anterior nasal septum and inferior/middle turbinates. The rationale is anatomical: the antero-inferior septum carries a rich anastomotic vascular plexus (Little area / Kiesselbach plexus) fed by the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries. This exposed, mucosa-thin area is easily traumatised, so the vast majority of accessible bleeds arise here and can be seen and treated directly.

Acute or recurrent nosebleed needing a source
Unilateral nasal obstruction or discharge
Assessment of septal deviation, perforation or turbinate hypertrophy
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Seat the patient upright, apply universal precautions, and use a headlight or head mirror to keep both hands free. Ask the patient to blow the nose (or gently suction) to clear clot, and consider a topical vasoconstrictor/anaesthetic spray (e.g. co-phenylcaine / lidocaine with a decongestant). Insert a Thudichum speculum, holding it so the blades open vertically, and inspect the septum, floor and lateral wall. Systematically look at Little area on the anterior septum first, then the turbinates, and observe the postnasal space for blood trickling down the pharynx.

Equipment: headlight, Thudichum speculum, suction, topical vasoconstrictor
Clear clot before inspecting so the bleeding point is not missed
Inspect Little area first, then turbinates and postnasal drip
3INTERPRETATION

The key decision is anterior versus posterior, because it changes management entirely.

Visible bleeding vessel on antero-inferior septum (Little area / Kiesselbach plexus)→Anterior epistaxis — amenable to silver nitrate cautery or anterior pack
No anterior source seen; blood trickling posteriorly down the pharynx, bleeding from both nares ± haemodynamic compromise→Posterior epistaxis (sphenopalatine artery) — needs posterior pack/balloon and admission
Unilateral blood-stained nasal discharge with a mass in an adult→Exclude sinonasal tumour — refer for imaging and ENT assessment
Unilateral obstruction & epistaxis in an adolescent male→Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma — image, do NOT biopsy
4PITFALLS & SAFETY

An unprepared examination on an uncleared, actively bleeding nose is the commonest reason a bleeding point is missed. Always consider systemic contributors — anticoagulants, antiplatelets, hypertension and inherited bleeding disorders — and check haemodynamic status in heavy bleeds. Never cauterise both sides of the septum at the same visit, as bilateral cautery risks septal perforation.

🧪Little area
Antero-inferior septal plexus; source of ~90% of bleeds
🩸Sphenopalatine artery
Main culprit in posterior, often torrential, epistaxis
💊Anticoagulation
Warfarin/DOAC/antiplatelet — check clotting and drug history
⚠️Unilateral mass
Red flag for tumour or angiofibroma — refer, do not biopsy blindly
🚩 Posterior epistaxis can cause significant, life-threatening haemorrhage — resuscitate (ABC, IV access, bloods including group & save), insert a posterior pack or balloon and admit. NEVER biopsy a suspected juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma: it is highly vascular and biopsy risks torrential bleeding. Always ask about bleeding disorders and anticoagulation.
🎓 Around 90% of nosebleeds are anterior, arising from Little area (Kiesselbach plexus). First aid: sit up, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of the nose continuously for 10–15 minutes while breathing through the mouth.
The mucosal-endoscopy, thyroid-cytology and sinus-imaging investigations.
1Flexible nasendoscopy / laryngoscopy
  • Persistent hoarseness >3 weeks (especially a smoker/drinker) → 2-week-wait ENT for laryngoscopy; also persistent sore throat, dysphagia, referred otalgia with a normal ear, or a non-healing oral ulcer.
  • A laryngeal mass / immobile cord → examination under anaesthesia + biopsy and cross-sectional staging. Head & neck cancer ›
New unilateral serous otitis media (glue ear) in an adult→examine the postnasal space (nasendoscopy) to exclude nasopharyngeal carcinoma (EBV-associated) → biopsy + EBV serology + MRI. Head & neck cancer ›
2Thyroid nodule: U & Thy grading
  • USS sonographic grade U1–U5 (U1 normal → U5 malignant) guides whether to FNA.
  • FNA cytology Thy1 non-diagnostic → repeat; Thy2 benign → reassure/discharge; Thy3 → diagnostic hemithyroidectomy; Thy4/Thy5 malignant → surgery/MDT. Thyroid cancer ›
Chronic rhinosinusitis / nasal polyps refractory to medical therapy, or pre-FESS→CT paranasal sinuses (maps the osteomeatal complex; Lund–Mackay) — not for acute uncomplicated sinusitis. Rhinosinusitis ›
Allergic rhinitis→skin-prick / serum specific IgE identifies the allergen → avoidance, intranasal steroid ± immunotherapy.
🎓 Exam pearl. Hoarseness >3 wks → 2WW nasendoscopy. Unilateral adult glue ear → exclude NPC. Thy2 reassure / Thy3 lobectomy / Thy4-5 cancer surgery. CT sinuses only if refractory CRS or pre-op.
